'''Joanne Chory''' (March 19, 1955 – November 12, 2024) was an American [[plant biology|plant biologist]] and [[geneticist]]. She was a professor and director of the Plant Molecular and Cellular Biology Laboratory at the [[Salk Institute for Biological Studies]] and an investigator of the [[Howard Hughes Medical Institute]].<ref name=":0">{{cite web|title = Professor Joanne Chory ForMemRS|url = http://www.salk.edu/faculty/chory.html|publisher = The Royal Society|access-date = 17 October 2013}}</ref>

Chory was the founding director of the Salk Institute's Harnessing Plants Initiative (HPI),<ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.salk.edu/harnessing-plants-initiative/ | title=Harnessing Plants Initiative }}</ref> a [[carbon dioxide removal]] approach to fight [[climate change]] by optimizing a plant's natural ability to capture and store carbon dioxide and adapt to different climate conditions. Chory and the HPI team aim to help plants grow bigger and stronger root systems that can absorb larger amounts of carbon by burying it in the ground in the form of [[suberin]], a naturally occurring substance.<ref name=":2">{{Cite web|last=|first=|date=|title=Joanne Chory: Professor and Director|url=https://www.salk.edu/scientist/joanne-chory/|archive-url=|archive-date=|access-date=|website=Salk}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news|last=Hahn|first=Jane|date=2021-04-28|title=Joanne Chory is using plants to save the planet|url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/climate-solutions/interactive/2021/joanne-chory-climate-plants/|access-date=2021-08-28|newspaper=Washington Post|language=en}}</ref> Chory and the HPI team received a $35 million award in support of the initiative from the [[The Audacious Project|TED Audacious Project]] in 2019 and another $30 million from the [[Bezos Earth Fund]] in 2020.<ref>{{Cite web |last= |first= |date= |title=TED Announces the 2019 Audacious Projects |url=https://sciencephilanthropyalliance.org/ted-announces-the-2019-audacious-projects-via-audaciousproject-org/ |archive-url= |archive-date= |access-date= |website=}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last= |first= |year=2020 |title=Bezos Earth Fund donates $30 million to Salk Institute for innovative climate change research |url=https://www.eurekalert.org/pub_releases/2020-11/si-bef111620.php |archive-url= |archive-date= |access-date= |website=Eurekalert}}</ref>

Chory's work at the Salk Institute, which she joined in 1988, pioneered the use of molecular genetics to study how plants change their shape and size to optimize [[photosynthesis]] and growth for different environments.<ref>{{Cite web|last=|first=|year=2020|title=Into the Light: A Profile of Joanne Chory|url=https://www.the-scientist.com/profile/into-the-light-a-profile-of-joanne-chory-67141|archive-url=|archive-date=|access-date=|website=The Scientist}}</ref><ref name=":2" /><ref>{{Cite web|last=|first=|date=|title=Ted2019. Joanne Chory: How supercharged plants could slow climate change|url=https://www.ted.com/speakers/joanne_chory|archive-url=|archive-date=|access-date=|website=Ted}}</ref> She held the Howard H. and Maryam R. Newman Chair in Plant Biology and was an adjunct professor in the Section of Cell and Developmental Biology at [[University of California, San Diego|UC San Diego]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Joanne Chory |url=http://biology.ucsd.edu/research/faculty/jchory |access-date=2015-09-26 |website=biology.ucsd.edu |archive-date=2015-09-25 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150925083152/http://biology.ucsd.edu/research/faculty/jchory |url-status=dead }}</ref>

Chory was elected as a [[Foreign Member of the Royal Society|foreign member]] of the [[Royal Society]] in 2011 and was the recipient of the 2018 [[Breakthrough Prize in Life Sciences]] and the 2019 [[Princess of Asturias Awards|Prince of Asturias Award]] for Technical and Scientific Research.<ref>{{Cite web|last=IT|first=Developed with webControl CMS by Intermark|title=Joanne Chory and Sandra Myrna Díaz – Laureates – Princess of Asturias Awards|url=https://www.fpa.es/en/princess-of-asturias-awards/laureates/2019-joanne-chory-and-sandra-myrna-diaz.html?especifica=0|access-date=2020-11-12|website=The Princess of Asturias Foundation|language=en}}</ref>

== Background ==
Chory was born in [[Boston|Boston, Massachusetts]], in 1955. Her Lebanese parents raised her along with her four brothers and one sister.<ref name=":3">{{Cite journal |last=Nemhauser |first=Jennifer L. |last2=Weigel |first2=Detlef |date=2025-07-23 |title=Joanne Chory (1955–2024): Plant geneticist extraordinaire |url=https://www.wikidata.org/wiki/Q135498886 |journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America |volume=122 |issue=30 |doi=10.1073/PNAS.2515437122|doi-access=free |pmc=12318232 }}</ref> She began her upper-level education at [[Oberlin College]] in Ohio where she graduated with a degree in biology with honors. She earned her PhD at [[University of Illinois at Urbana–Champaign|University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign]].<ref name=":1">{{Cite web|url=https://www.hhmi.org/insidelook/joanne-chory|title=Joanne Chory|website=HHMI.org|language=en|access-date=2019-02-28}}</ref><ref name=":3" />

She was a postdoctoral fellow at the [[Harvard Medical School]] in the lab of [[Frederick M. Ausubel]].<ref name="Salk">{{cite web|url=http://www.salk.edu/faculty/chory.html|title=Joanne Chory|publisher=[[Salk Institute for Biological Studies]]|access-date=17 October 2013}}</ref> In 1988 she joined the [[Salk Institute for Biological Studies|Salk Institute]] as an assistant professor. Chory eventually married her husband, Stephen Worland, with whom she has two adopted children.

In 2004, Chory was diagnosed with [[Parkinson's disease]]. She struggled with the disease for well over a decade, but with the help of medications and a brain implant to help regulate her movement, she  continued her genetic research. Along with her passion for genetics, Chory strived to inspire young women to become scientists and constantly worked to improve the field for women.<ref name=":1" />

Chory's early career interests were centered in microbiology. Through her research in that field she developed a deeper interest in genetics, specifically research that was being done on Arabidopsis plants. Through her lengthy career in genetics she was awarded numerous accolades for her many contributions to the field.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.newswise.com/|title=Newswise: News for Journalists|website=www.newswise.com|access-date=2019-02-28}}</ref>

Chory died from complications of Parkinson's disease in [[La Jolla, California]], on November 12, 2024, at the age of 69.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.salk.edu/news-release/joanne-chory-salk-institute-professor-and-pioneering-plant-biologist-dies-at-age-69/|title=Joanne Chory, Salk Institute professor and pioneering plant biologist, dies at age 69|publisher=Salk.edu|accessdate=November 13, 2024|date=November 13, 2024}}</ref>

== Career and research ==
Chory focused her research on finding a way to optimize plant growth to sustain a growing human population. She used ''[[Arabidopsis thaliana]]'' as a [[model organism]], but her purpose was to optimize all plant growth and not just that of ''A. thaliana'' itself. She mutated the genes of the model organism and used the results to understand the effects that these mutations have. She approached this information from various directions including using genetics, genomics, cell biology, x-ray crystallography, biochemistry, and ecology. She made strides in understanding light sensitivity and hormones in these plants. She used this knowledge to optimize growth in other plants in hopes that the work will help  sustain an ever-growing human population.<ref name=":0" />

Chory showed particular appreciation for manipulation of phenotypes of an organism.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Bartel|first=B.|date=2012-06-01|title=The 2012 Genetics Society of America Medal: Joanne Chory|journal=Genetics|language=en|volume=191|issue=2|pages=297–298|doi=10.1534/genetics.112.138404|issn=0016-6731|pmc=3374298|pmid=22701045}}</ref> Light signals are required for the induction and regulation of many developmental processes in plants. She  participated in research dissecting this complex process by isolating mutations that alter light-regulated seedling development in [[Arabidopsis thaliana|Arabidopsis]].<ref>{{Cite journal|title = Arabidopsis thaliana mutant that develops as a light-grown plant in the absence of light|journal = Cell|date = 1989-09-08|pages = 991–999|volume = 58|issue = 5|doi = 10.1016/0092-8674(89)90950-1|pmid = 2776216|first1 = Joanne|last1 = Chory|first2 = Charles|last2 = Peto|first3 = Rhonda|last3 = Feinbaum|first4 = Lee|last4 = Pratt|first5 = Frederick|last5 = Ausubel|s2cid = 39355835}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|title = DET1, a negative regulator of light-mediated development and gene expression in arabidopsis, encodes a novel nuclear-localized protein|journal = Cell|date = 1994-07-15|pages = 109–116|volume = 78|issue = 1|doi = 10.1016/0092-8674(94)90577-0|first1 = Alan|last1 = Pepper|first2 = Terrence|last2 = Delaney|first3 = Tracy|last3 = Washburnt|first4 = Daniel|last4 = Poole|first5 = Joanne|last5 = Chory|pmid = 8033202|s2cid = 42247168}}</ref> Her work identified mutants that are deficient in the phytochrome photoreceptors and in nuclear-localized repressors and also revealed that steroid hormones control light-regulated seedling development. Dr. Chory's lab has been involved in the manipulation of the biosynthetic pathway for these steroids that altered the growth and development of plants and identification of the putative steroid receptor, a transmembrane receptor kinase.<ref>{{Cite journal|title = A Putative Leucine-Rich Repeat Receptor Kinase Involved in Brassinosteroid Signal Transduction|journal = Cell|date =
